paragraphs: The paper addresses learning when data is plentiful, as in object recognition and language modeling. In this setting, the challenge is to design algorithms that can make effective use of the available examples. The authors emphasize that learning and optimization become different tasks: a powerful method for optimizing an objective can still be a suboptimal learning algorithm.

They bring together two research directions. One adapts optimization methods to learning by efficiently using the Hessian, which describes how an objective’s curvature changes across parameter directions. The other exploits the special structure of the learning problem, an approach that earlier work used to obtain faster convergence. These directions suggest complementary ways to guide learning updates.

The paper investigates a natural combination of these ideas aimed at producing fast, robust learning algorithms. Its central contribution, as described in the abstract, is this combined direction. The stated motivation is that algorithm design should account for both optimization information and the structure of learning when abundant data makes their distinction consequential.
icml-2010-a-fast-natural-newton-method-d.tldr: The paper investigates combining Hessian information with the special structure of learning problems to develop fast, robust algorithms for settings with abundant data.

paragraphs: The paper introduces and derives a new stick-breaking construction of the beta process. A construction provides an explicit way to build the mathematical object used by a model, making its structure available for further algorithmic development. Here, the authors connect their construction to a special case of the Dirichlet process stick-breaking construction applied to the beta distribution.

That connection is central to the contribution: the proposed construction develops a relationship between two probabilistic constructions rather than simply presenting an unrelated recipe. The paper also moves from the construction to inference, deriving a procedure for working with the resulting model. This procedure uses Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of parameters that must be inferred.

Reducing the inference burden gives the mathematical construction a practical role. The authors present results on synthetic data, handwritten digits from MNIST, and gene expression data that evolve over time. These applications illustrate the method across different data settings. The stated contribution combines a new representation, its derivation, and an inference procedure supported by application results.
icml-2010-a-stick-breaking-construction-.tldr: A new stick-breaking construction of the beta process leads to an inference procedure that uses Monte Carlo integration to reduce the number of inferred parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to measure the risk of an existing model while paying for as few labels as possible. Ordinary evaluation using held-out training data may be unavailable or inappropriate when those data do not represent the intended test population. The authors instead start with a pool of unlabeled test examples and choose which examples to label.

Their approach makes sampling an active part of evaluation. Rather than treating every candidate as equally useful, it asks which sampling distribution minimizes the estimation error of the active risk estimator. The paper derives that distribution and analyzes the distribution governing the estimator to obtain confidence intervals. These intervals express uncertainty around the resulting risk estimate.

The empirical comparison holds the number of labeled examples equal between active estimation and standard sampling from the test distribution. The authors study conditions under which active selection produces a more accurate estimate. The contribution therefore concerns efficient assessment of a given model, with an advantage that depends on the conditions examined rather than a universal improvement.
icml-2010-active-risk-estimation-328084c.tldr: Active risk estimation selects test examples to label and derives an error-minimizing sampling distribution and confidence intervals for evaluating a given model.

paragraphs: The paper develops classifiers tailored to individual patients to detect when an epileptic seizure begins. The input is scalp EEG, a non-invasive recording of the brain’s electrical activity. Detection is difficult because seizure activity must be distinguished from numerous other forms of brain activity whose characteristics overlap.

The authors identify two central parts of their approach: framing the detection problem appropriately for machine learning and finding features that separate seizures from other activity. Training uses at least two seizures from each patient. This patient-specific setup is part of the reported evaluation, so the findings describe detection after learning from seizure examples for the person being monitored.

Testing covered 916 hours of continuous EEG from 24 patients. The algorithm detected 96% of 173 test seizures, with a median delay of 3 seconds and a median of 2 false detections per 24 hours. Together, these measures describe detection coverage, timeliness, and false alerts. The paper also provides access information for the CHB-MIT database containing the study data.
icml-2010-application-of-machine-learnin.tldr: Patient-specific EEG classifiers detected 96% of test seizures, with a median 3-second delay and 2 false detections per day in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Transfer learning aims to improve learning on a new target problem by using knowledge from related source problems. This paper addresses that goal for regression, where the prediction is a numerical value. Its stated contribution is the first set of boosting-based transfer learning algorithms that applies to regression tasks.

The authors begin with ExpBoost and TrAdaBoost, two existing transfer algorithms for classification. They explain how these methods can be modified for regression, extending their use beyond predicting categories. This provides a route from established classification transfer methods to the numerical prediction setting, while retaining boosting as the basis of the algorithms.

The paper then introduces extensions to the adapted methods and reports significant performance improvements in controlled experiments across a wide range of test domains. Those findings support the value of the proposed extensions in the evaluated settings. The overall contribution has two parts: making boosting-based transfer available for regression and improving those methods through further algorithmic development.
icml-2010-boosting-for-regression-transf.tldr: The paper adapts boosting-based transfer methods to regression and introduces extensions that significantly improve performance in controlled experiments.

paragraphs: The paper uses relationships among human languages as a source of information for learning. Its central idea is that these relationships can provide naturally occurring supervision: structure shared or linked across languages can help guide a model. The authors develop a class of probabilistic models around this multilingual learning approach.

They report substantial performance improvements on several core language-processing tasks. These include morphological segmentation, which concerns the meaningful pieces within words; part-of-speech tagging, which assigns grammatical categories; and syntactic parsing, which identifies sentence structure. The range of tasks matters because the contribution is presented as a broader modeling approach rather than a method for only one linguistic prediction.

The paper also presents a multilingual model for computational decipherment of lost languages. This extends the use of cross-language relationships beyond the traditional tasks considered in the study. Taken together, the contributions show how probabilistic models can make linguistic connections useful as learning signals, with reported gains on established tasks and a further application to decipherment.
icml-2010-climbing-the-tower-of-babel-un.tldr: Probabilistic multilingual models use relationships among languages as natural supervision, improving core language tasks and supporting a model for deciphering lost languages.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when each item is a sample generated by a process. Its target is to group samples exactly according to their generating distributions. The authors formalize an asymptotic notion of consistency: samples belong together if and only if the same distribution generated them. This connects clustering to testing whether samples share a distribution and to process classification.

When the number of clusters is known, consistent algorithms require only that the joint data distribution be stationary and ergodic. The result does not require a parametric model, a Markov assumption, or independence within or between samples. This makes the guarantee applicable to a broad class of dependent data under the stated process assumption.

When the number of clusters is unknown, consistency requires additional conditions on mixing rates, which concern how dependence evolves over separation. The authors provide simple consistent algorithms for both settings, with at most quadratic complexity in each argument. The guarantees are asymptotic, establishing eventual clustering correctness under their respective assumptions.
icml-2010-clustering-processes-561f19f03.tldr: The paper establishes consistent clustering of process-generated samples under broad dependence assumptions, with stronger conditions needed when the cluster count is unknown.

paragraphs: COFFIN addresses a scaling problem in support vector machines: applying a conventional kernel SVM becomes slower as the number of support vectors grows. This creates a barrier to very large applications even when kernels provide useful representations. The paper develops a training strategy for linear SVMs intended to make sophisticated feature representations practical at that scale.

The framework allows kernel feature spaces to be computed on demand and supports virtual examples within primal training. Its stated computational benefit is linear training and prediction effort. The approach connects rich representations with a linear SVM training strategy, allowing the authors to tackle datasets containing millions of examples.

The demonstrations include human splice-site recognition with 50 million examples and sophisticated string kernels, plus gender detection with 5 million examples on low-tech hardware. The authors report accuracy exceeding the previous state of the art on both tasks. These results support both the framework’s large-scale practicality and its predictive performance in those applications. Code, datasets, and scripts were also made freely available.
icml-2010-coffin-a-computational-framewo.tldr: COFFIN enables large-scale linear SVM training with on-demand kernel features, demonstrated on tasks containing 50 million and 5 million examples.

paragraphs: Approximate dynamic programming represents solutions using a supplied set of features. Richer feature sets can express more, but limited samples create a risk of overfitting. This paper addresses the resulting tension: providing many potentially useful features can make existing algorithms less reliable instead of improving their solutions.

The authors introduce L1 regularization into approximate linear programming for Markov decision processes. The method automatically controls the richness of the features used, rather than requiring a small feature set to be chosen beforehand. They report that performance does not deteriorate as the number of available features increases, with this result resting on new, stronger sampling bounds for the regularized formulation.

The paper also proposes a computationally efficient homotopy method, addressing how to solve the resulting problem in practice. Empirical evaluation shows good performance on simple Markov decision processes and standard benchmarks. The contribution combines feature selection, sampling theory, and computation, making larger collections of candidate features usable within the proposed approximate planning approach.
icml-2010-feature-selection-using-regula.tldr: L1-regularized approximate linear programming automatically controls feature richness, supported by stronger sampling bounds and an efficient homotopy method.

paragraphs: This paper examines the computational work needed to scale variational approximate inference for sparse linear models. Gaussian covariance calculations are central to that work because they represent posterior dependencies, yet approximating them is computationally difficult. The authors focus on how choices made to simplify these calculations affect the usefulness of the resulting inference.

Many earlier approaches obtain scalability by leaving most posterior dependencies unrepresented. The paper considers data-dependent low-rank covariance approximations as a way to avoid harmful factorization assumptions. This changes the approximation strategy: dependencies can remain represented through a more compact covariance description, although that description still introduces approximation error.

The authors study the algorithmic and statistical consequences of those errors using both theory and empirical analysis. Their setting is nonlinear sequential Bayesian experimental design, where inferred uncertainty influences decisions about experiments. This makes the consequences concrete: covariance approximations matter through the decisions they produce. The contribution explains the connection between computational shortcuts, uncertainty representation, and downstream decision outcomes.
icml-2010-gaussian-covariance-and-scalab.tldr: The paper analyzes how data-dependent low-rank covariance approximations enable scalable inference and affect decisions in sequential Bayesian experimental design.

paragraphs: Time series can contain both relationships across nearby observations and abrupt changes between regimes. This paper combines Gaussian processes with Bayesian online change-point detection to accommodate both. The resulting nonparametric model can locate changes as observations arrive while accounting for temporal correlations within a regime.

That combination matters because a change-detection method must describe what ordinary behavior within a regime looks like. Here, observations within a regime can be temporally correlated, a setting that the authors distinguish from other Bayesian online change-point algorithms. Gaussian processes provide the component used to represent this within-regime behavior while the change-point framework handles transitions.

The paper develops three ways to apply Gaussian processes in this context, each with its own advantages. It also presents methods for reducing their computational burden and demonstrates the approach on several real-world datasets. The contribution therefore includes a modeling combination, alternative formulations, and computational improvements, all directed toward online analysis of time series that have both temporal structure and regime changes.
icml-2010-gaussian-process-change-point-.tldr: Combining Gaussian processes with Bayesian online change-point detection allows regime changes to be located while modeling temporal correlations within regimes.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization of an unknown function whose evaluations are noisy and expensive. It models this as a bandit problem under two alternative descriptions of the payoff function: a sample from a Gaussian process, or a function with low reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space norm. These assumptions provide the structure needed for the analysis.

The authors analyze GP-UCB, which uses upper confidence estimates to guide evaluation choices. They bound cumulative regret, the accumulated cost of choosing points below the optimum, through maximal information gain. This establishes a connection to experimental design: the information obtainable from evaluations helps characterize the difficulty of optimization.

Bounds on information gain through operator spectra yield explicit sublinear regret bounds for many commonly used covariance functions. These results imply convergence rates, and some important cases have only weak dependence on dimension. Experiments using real sensor data also show favorable comparisons with heuristic GP optimization methods. The theoretical guarantees and empirical findings provide distinct support for the algorithm under the settings studied.
icml-2010-gaussian-process-optimization-.tldr: GP-UCB receives regret and convergence guarantees by linking Gaussian process optimization to information gain and experimental design.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models describe sequence data through hidden states and observations. The paper identifies restrictions in conventional models, including discrete latent states and observation models largely confined to Gaussian or discrete distributions. It also highlights that most HMM learning algorithms rely on local search, which motivates a different approach to fitting the model.

The authors propose a nonparametric HMM based on Hilbert-space embeddings that extends the framework to structured and non-Gaussian continuous distributions. They derive a kernel spectral learning algorithm that is free of local minima. The contribution therefore changes both what distributions the model can represent and how the model is learned.

Evaluation uses robot vision, slot-car inertial sensors, and audio event classification. The embedded HMMs exceed the previous state-of-the-art performance in these applications. These results support the usefulness of the representation and learning method across several sequence-data settings. The reported performance advantage applies to those applications, while the local-minimum-free property is a separate characteristic of the proposed learning algorithm.
icml-2010-hilbert-space-embeddings-of-hi.tldr: A nonparametric embedded HMM supports richer distributions and a local-minimum-free kernel spectral learner, outperforming prior methods in three reported applications.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often starts with an agent’s reward already specified and asks how the agent can pursue it effectively. This paper expands the design problem to include the choice of that reward. It distinguishes the agent’s internal goal from the designer’s goal, then asks which internal rewards best serve what the designer ultimately wants.

The motivation is that practical agents have computational bounds. A reward that guides a limited agent well may improve its performance against the designer’s objective. The authors express reward selection as a meta-optimization problem: the design process chooses the internal objective, while the agent learns or acts according to that objective.

The paper supplies a formal framework for both bounded agents and this additional optimization problem. It also empirically demonstrates several cases in which general internal reward functions mitigate common agent bounds. The stated claim is that well-designed internal rewards can help computationally bounded agents. The examples support that possibility without establishing that every reward redesign or every agent bound will benefit.
icml-2010-internal-rewards-mitigate-agen.tldr: Choosing an agent’s internal rewards to serve the designer’s objective can mitigate computational limitations, as shown in a formal framework and empirical examples.

paragraphs: Deep Boltzmann machines can define distributions with many separated local modes when modeling richly structured, high-dimensional data. The paper describes this as a rough energy landscape with high barriers. A commonly used Gibbs sampler can become trapped in one mode, often causing unstable learning and poor parameter estimates.

The authors investigate adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo methods as a way to address that sampling problem. They first establish a close connection between Fast PCD and adaptive MCMC. They then introduce Coupled Adaptive Simulated Tempering, an algorithm designed to explore a highly multimodal energy landscape more effectively.

The key connection is between exploration during sampling and the quality of learned model parameters. If sampling remains confined to one mode, learning can be adversely affected; the proposed method targets that difficulty directly. The authors demonstrate considerable improvement in parameter estimates, particularly for large-scale deep Boltzmann machines. This is an empirical improvement in the learning setting studied, rather than a claim that all multimodal sampling problems are resolved.
icml-2010-learning-deep-boltzmann-machin.tldr: Coupled Adaptive Simulated Tempering improves exploration during deep Boltzmann machine learning and considerably improves parameter estimates in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A ranked list can contain individually useful documents yet still disappoint users because the results repeat one another. This paper attributes that problem to treating each document’s usefulness as independent of the others. It develops a learning-to-rank formulation that explicitly accounts for document similarity and the context created by the ranking.

The objective is to maximize the fraction of satisfied users. This makes the collection of results central to the learning problem: a document’s contribution depends on the other documents returned. The authors provide theoretical justification for the formulation and a near-optimal algorithm, addressing the lack of foundations or scalability they identify in earlier approaches.

The evaluation includes additional optimizations that improve empirical performance. It also reports that the proposed algorithms learn orders of magnitude faster than previous approaches. The contribution brings together an objective centered on user satisfaction, an explicit treatment of redundancy, and scalable learning. The near-optimality claim concerns the proposed formulation, while the speed advantage is a reported empirical finding.
icml-2010-learning-optimally-diverse-ran.tldr: A theoretically supported ranking formulation accounts for redundancy and user satisfaction, with a near-optimal algorithm and much faster learning in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning appears well positioned to spread information from experience and guide exploration. Yet the paper identifies a mismatch between that intuition and available guarantees. For finite Markov decision processes with N states, the best stated model-based exploration bounds were O(N² log N), compared with O(N log N) for model-free delayed Q-learning.

The authors introduce MoRmax, a modified version of Rmax, and prove an upper bound of O(N log N) exploratory steps. This closes the stated gap in dependence on the number of states between the model-based guarantee and the existing model-free guarantee. The result concerns the number of exploratory actions needed to learn a good policy.

The new bound matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors and improves dependence on other problem parameters. Its significance is theoretical: model-based learning can attain a nearly tight exploration guarantee rather than retaining the previously worse state-count dependence. Matching the model-free upper bound establishes comparable exploration guarantees, rather than proving that model-based methods always explore less.
icml-2010-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: MoRmax achieves an O(N log N) exploration bound, matching the stated model-free upper bound and approaching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: The paper presents a musical accompaniment system in which a computer-driven orchestra follows and learns from a soloist. The setting resembles a concerto, with the accompaniment responding to an ongoing performance. The system separates this task into three modules that handle score matching, sound generation, and prediction of future timing.

A hidden Markov model determines the real-time match between the performance and the score. A second module generates accompaniment audio by applying phase vocoding to an existing recording. Between them, a Kalman filter-like model predicts how timing will evolve, connecting the estimate of the soloist’s current progress to the audio that should follow.

This architecture matters because following a performer requires both tracking the present and anticipating what comes next. The paper presents examples in diverse musical settings to show the system operating. It also discusses connections to machine learning, identifies current weaknesses, and points toward possible new directions. The contribution is an integrated accompaniment system illustrated through performance examples.
icml-2010-music-plus-one-and-machine-lea.tldr: A computer accompaniment system combines real-time score tracking, recorded-audio transformation, and timing prediction to follow a soloist.

paragraphs: This paper studies online prediction using advice from multiple experts when their performance information is private. Each expert observes its own loss at each step, but confidentiality prevents sharing that loss with others. The challenge is to use those private values to guide prediction without requiring their disclosure.

The authors develop a secure version of exponential weighting using cryptographic tools. Exponential weighting uses expert losses to determine how their advice contributes to prediction; the secure scheme enables those losses to be used under the privacy restriction. This preserves the role of performance feedback even though participants cannot openly exchange it.

The paper proves that the secure scheme has the same, or almost the same, regret bound as conventional exponential weighting in the full-information setting. It separately proves privacy in the formal sense of secure function evaluation. These are complementary guarantees: one concerns prediction performance over time, while the other concerns confidentiality during computation. The result connects a private information setting to familiar online-learning performance bounds.
icml-2010-online-prediction-with-privacy.tldr: Cryptographic exponential weighting uses experts’ private losses while retaining the same or nearly the same regret bounds and providing secure-function-evaluation privacy.

paragraphs: This paper compares two ways to evaluate a policy using a linear approximation of its value function in a Markov decision process. One computes the TD(0) fixed point; the other minimizes the Bellman residual. The authors give examples where each method beats the other, showing that their relative quality can depend on the problem.

They identify a simple relationship between the objectives and establish that Bellman-residual minimization has a performance guarantee that TD(0) lacks in general. They then express both approaches as oblique projections of the Bellman equation. This shared mathematical view simplifies and extends earlier characterizations, making the methods easier to analyze within one framework.

Simulations suggest a distinction between typical performance and average performance. TD(0) solutions are usually slightly better in those simulations, but numerical instability produces very poor outcomes in some cases, making TD(0) worse on average. The finding highlights how occasional severe failures can outweigh a modest usual advantage; it remains a simulation-based observation rather than a universal ranking.
icml-2010-should-one-compute-the-tempora.tldr: A unified projection analysis compares TD(0) and Bellman-residual minimization, revealing different guarantees and simulation evidence that TD instability can outweigh its usual slight advantage.

paragraphs: The Spherical Admixture Model is a Bayesian topic model for data normalized to have unit L2 length. It retains the hierarchical structure of Latent Dirichlet Allocation while changing how documents are represented. Documents become points on a high-dimensional sphere, allowing the likelihood to be parameterized naturally through cosine distance.

This geometric choice connects the model to the directions of normalized data vectors. The model also permits topics to give terms negative weights. According to the authors, this enables it to represent information about both word presence and word absence, extending the expressive capabilities of the previous models they discuss.

The evaluation examines the model from two perspectives. Human raters assess it as a topic model, while classification experiments span natural language processing and computer vision. This range reflects the model’s applicability to arbitrary L2-normalized data, beyond its document-based motivation. The contribution is a new topic-model formulation and an empirical evaluation of its interpretability and predictive use across different tasks.
icml-2010-spherical-topic-models-9f4734d.tldr: The Spherical Admixture Model represents normalized data on a sphere and allows negative topic weights to capture word absence as well as presence.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a classifier when individual observations have no known labels, but label frequencies are available for some groups of observations. This supplies more information than fully unlabeled data while providing less detail than ordinary supervised examples. The objective is still to learn a classifier from that aggregate information.

The proposed approach combines support vector regression with the idea of reversing classifier calibration. Calibration ordinarily connects classifier outputs with probabilities; the authors use an inverted calibration perspective to help estimate a classifier from group probabilities. The method therefore turns group-level label information into a basis for learning despite the absence of individual labels.

The authors identify privacy-preserving data mining as an important application of this learning setting and report that a detailed analysis shows their approach outperforming existing methods. The contribution is a specific route from aggregate supervision to classifier estimation. Its practical relevance comes from using information available at the group level, while the reported comparative result supports the proposed approach in the paper’s analysis.
icml-2010-svm-classifier-estimation-from.tldr: Support vector regression and inverted classifier calibration enable classifier learning from group-level label frequencies without individual training labels.

paragraphs: The Margin Perceptron with Unlearning modifies the classical margin-based Perceptron by allowing some previous contributions to its weight vector to shrink. During an ordinary update, the method can reduce contributions associated with examples that are already very well classified. Here, unlearning describes this adjustment within training.

The resulting method remains an incremental classification algorithm. The authors prove that it reaches a chosen approximation of either the maximum-margin solution or the optimal 1-norm soft-margin solution after finitely many updates. The desired approximation is selected before running the algorithm, making the target accuracy part of the procedure’s setup.

This result connects a relatively direct update mechanism with optimization targets associated with margin-based classification. The paper also compares the method experimentally with representative linear support vector machines and reports that it is highly competitive. The theoretical result establishes finite convergence to the specified approximation, while the experiments address practical comparative performance. Together, they support unlearning as a useful modification to the margin Perceptron.
icml-2010-the-margin-perceptron-with-unl.tldr: The Margin Perceptron with Unlearning reduces contributions from well-classified examples and provably reaches a preselected approximation to margin-optimal solutions in finitely many updates.

paragraphs: Clinical risk prediction often relies on labeled examples of patients who did and did not experience an adverse outcome. Such training data are difficult to collect when the outcome is rare. This paper proposes an unsupervised approach that identifies higher-risk patients without requiring those positive and negative training labels.

The method uses anomaly detection, employing a minimum enclosing ball to identify cases in sparse regions of the feature space. Its organizing idea is that unusual patient profiles can provide a signal for risk stratification. The authors describe the method as requiring no expert knowledge, so its risk grouping is derived from the data representation and anomaly-detection procedure.

Evaluation covers patients admitted with acute coronary syndrome and patients undergoing inpatient surgery. The method successfully identifies individuals at increased risk of adverse endpoints in both populations. In some cases it outperforms other machine learning methods supplied with labeled examples. These findings support unsupervised risk stratification in the evaluated populations, with the comparative advantage explicitly limited to some cases.
icml-2010-unsupervised-risk-stratificati.tldr: Unsupervised anomaly detection identified higher-risk patients in two clinical populations without labeled training examples, sometimes outperforming methods that used labels.

paragraphs: Choosing variables for clustering is difficult because there are no class labels to identify the desired grouping. This paper highlights a further complication: high-dimensional data can have several meaningful structures, each visible through a different subset of attributes. Searching for a single supposedly best subset may therefore overlook useful ways to understand the data.

The authors propose helping domain experts select among clustering alternatives. The system identifies different facets of a dataset, clusters observations along each facet, and presents those results for expert appraisal. To support this approach, the paper introduces a generalization of the Gaussian mixture model and shows that it can cluster data along multiple facets.

The contribution changes the role of variable selection from producing one final answer to exposing meaningful alternatives. Different attribute subsets become ways of revealing different structures that experts can assess. The authors demonstrate that facilitating selection is often more reasonable than performing it automatically. This is a qualified argument about multifaceted data, rather than a claim that automatic variable selection is never appropriate.
icml-2010-variable-selection-in-model-ba.tldr: A generalized Gaussian mixture model reveals multiple clustering facets so domain experts can choose among meaningful attribute subsets and groupings.
